ld.description: Flat-fee condominium, HOA, and townhome association management in Chicago, starting at $20 per unit per month.

offers.description: Starting price; final flat monthly fee is based on the agreed association management scope.

mainEntity.name: How much does condo association management cost in Chicago?

acceptedAnswer.text: Stellar management pricing starts at $20 per unit per month. The final flat monthly fee depends on the association’s size, building systems, staffing, amenities, financial complexity, meeting schedule, and agreed service scope.

mainEntity.name: Is $20 per unit the final price for every association?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. It is our starting price, not a universal quote. We review the property, financials, governing documents, current contracts, and board priorities before presenting a flat monthly proposal tailored to the association.

mainEntity.name: Does Stellar charge a capital-project oversight fee?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Stellar does not add a separate capital-project planning or management-oversight fee. That management work is included in the agreed service scope. Contractor, engineer, architect, legal, permit, and other third-party project costs remain association expenses.

mainEntity.name: Is the fee based on a percentage of our association budget?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Stellar quotes a transparent flat monthly management fee. Our compensation does not increase simply because your association budget or capital-project spending increases.

mainEntity.name: Can our board compare Stellar’s proposal with our current contract?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. We encourage boards to compare total annual cost, included services, add-on fees, termination terms, manager assignment, and transition support—not just the headline monthly number.

What determines your exact fee?
blocks.cls: font-display font-light text-4xl lg:text-5xl text-ink leading-[1.08] mb-8

blocks.html: Two associations with the same unit count can require very different levels of management. We inspect the property and define the workload before quoting, so your board can evaluate a complete scope instead of discovering add-ons later.
Community size
Unit count helps establish the baseline workload and per-unit economics.
Building operations
Amenities, elevators, mechanical systems, staffing, and vendor coordination shape the scope.
Financial complexity
Budgeting, collections, reserves, reporting, and active projects affect the support required.
Board service needs
Meeting cadence, communications, governance support, and transition needs are defined before quoting.
Included Management
